entries.cacc4bf0d56af82986ccd9f319d14052ebe74da8: <div sID="gen16262" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="36" osisID="Isa.36" sID="Isa.36"/> <div eID="gen16262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16263" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16264" type="x-p"/> The prophet Isaiah is, in this and the three following chapters, an historian; for the scripture history, as well as the scripture prophecy, is given by inspiration of God, and was dictated to holy men. Many of the prophecies of the foregoing chapters had their accomplishment in Sennacherib's invading Judah and besieging Jerusalem, and the miraculous defeat he met with there; and therefore the story of this is here inserted, both for the explication and for the confirmation of the prophecy. The key of prophecy is to be found in history; and here, that we might have the readier entrance, it is, as it were, hung at the door. The exact fulfilling of this prophecy might serve to confirm the faith of God's people in the other prophecies, the accomplishment of which was at a greater distance. Whether this story was taken from the book of the Kings and added here, or whether it was first written by Isaiah here and hence taken into the book of Kings, is not material. But the story is the same almost verbatim; and it was so memorable an event that it was well worthy to be twice recorded, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.1-2Kgs.19.37">2 Kings xviii. and xix.</reference>, and here, and an abridgment of it likewise, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.1-2Chr.32.33">2 Chron. xxxii.</reference> We shall be but short in our observations upon this story here, having largely explained it there. In this chapter we have, I. The descent which the king of Assyria made upon Judah, and his success against all the defenced cities, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. The conference he desired to have with Hezekiah, and the managers on both sides, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.2-Isa.36.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>. III. Rabshakeh's railing blasphemous speech, with which he designed to frighten Hezekiah into a submission, and persuade him to surrender at discretion, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.4-Isa.36.10">ver. 4-10</reference>. IV. His appeal to the people, and his attempt to persuade them to desert Hezekiah, and so force him to surrender, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.11-Isa.36.20">ver. 11-20</reference>. V. The report of this made to Hezekiah by his agents, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.21-Isa.36.22">ver. 21, 22</reference>.
entries.4127a6a1a746874ea0f35c311992fb9d0c58b4b4: <div eID="gen16264" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16263" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Sennacherib's Insolent Message. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen16265" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now it came to pass in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah, <hi type="italic">that</hi> Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the defenced cities of Judah, and took them. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the king of Assyria sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem unto king Hezekiah with a great army. And he stood by the conduit of the upper pool in the highway of the fuller's field. <hi type="super">3</hi> Then came forth unto him Eliakim, Hilkiah's son, which was over the house, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah, Asaph's son, the recorder. <hi type="super">4</hi> And Rabshakeh said unto them, Say ye now to Hezekiah, Thus saith the great king, the king of Assyria, What confidence <hi type="italic">is</hi> this wherein thou trustest? <hi type="super">5</hi> I say, <hi type="italic">sayest thou,</hi> (but <hi type="italic">they are but</hi> vain words) <hi type="italic">I have</hi> counsel and strength for war: now on whom dost thou trust, that thou rebellest against me? <hi type="super">6</hi> Lo, thou trustest in the staff of this broken reed, on Egypt; whereon if a man lean, it will go into his hand, and pierce it: so <hi type="italic">is</hi> Pharaoh king of Egypt to all that trust in him. <hi type="super">7</hi> But if thou say to me, We trust in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God: <hi type="italic">is it</hi> not he, whose high places and whose altars Hezekiah hath taken away, and said to Judah and to Jerusalem, Ye shall worship before this altar? <hi type="super">8</hi> Now therefore give pledges, I pray thee, to my master the king of Assyria, and I will give thee two thousand horses, if thou be able on thy part to set riders upon them. <hi type="super">9</hi> How then wilt thou turn away the face of one captain of the least of my master's servants, and put thy trust on Egypt for chariots and for horsemen? <hi type="super">10</hi> And am I now come up without the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> against this land to destroy it? the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto me, Go up against this land, and destroy it. <div eID="gen16265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16266" type="x-p"/> We shall here only observe some practical lessons. 1. A people may be in the way of their duty and yet meet with trouble and distress. Hezekiah was reforming, and his people were in some measure reformed; and yet their country is at that time invaded and a great part of it laid waste. Perhaps they began to grow remiss and cool in the work of reformation, were doing it by halves, and ready to sit down short of a thorough reformation; and then God visited them with this judgment, to put life into them and that good cause. We must not wonder if, when we are doing well, God sends afflictions to quicken us to do better, to do our best, and to press forward towards perfection. 2. That we must never be secure of the continuance of our peace in this world, nor think our mountain stands so strong that it cannot be moved. Hezekiah was not only a pious king, but prudent, both in his administration at home and in his treaties abroad. His affairs were in a good posture, and he seemed particularly to be upon good terms with the king of Assyria, for he had lately made his peace with him by a rich present (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.14">2 Kings xviii. 14</reference>), and yet that perfidious prince pours an army into his country all of a sudden and lays it waste. It is good for us therefore always to keep up an expectation of trouble, that, when it comes, it may be no surprise to us, and then it will be the less a terror. 3. God sometimes permits the enemies of his people, even those that are most impious and treacherous, to prevail far against them. The king of Assyria took all, or most, of the defenced cities of Judah, and then the country would of course be an easy prey to him. Wickedness may prosper awhile, but cannot prosper always. 4. Proud men love to talk big, to boast of what they are, and have, and have done, nay and of what they will do, to insult over others, and set all mankind at defiance, though thereby they render themselves ridiculous to all wise men and obnoxious to the wrath of that God who resists the proud. But thus they think to make themselves feared, though they make themselves hated, and to carry their point by <hi type="italic">great swelling words</hi> of vanity, <reference osisRef="Jude.1.16">Jude 16</reference>. 5. The enemies of God's people endeavour to conquer them by frightening them, especially by frightening them from their confidence in God. Thus Rabshakeh here, with noise and banter, runs down Hezekiah as utterly unable to cope with his master, or in the least to make head against him. It concerns us therefore, that we may keep our ground against the enemies of our souls, to keep up our spirits by keeping up our hope in God. 6. It is acknowledged, on all hands, that those who forsake God's service forfeit his protection. If that had been true which Rabshakeh alleged, that Hezekiah had thrown down God's altars, he might justly infer that he could not with any assurance trust in him for succour and relief, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.7">v. 7</reference>, We may say thus to presuming sinners, who say that they trust in the Lord and in his mercy. Is not this he whose commandments they have lived in the contempt of, whose name they have dishonoured, and whose ordinances they have slighted? How then can they expect to find favour with him? 7. It is an easy thing, and very common, for those that persecute the church and people of God to pretend a commission from him for so doing. Rabshakeh could say, <hi type="italic">Have I now come up without the Lord?</hi> when really he had come up <hi type="italic">against</hi> the Lord, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.28">ch. xxxvii. 28</reference>. Those that kill the servants of the Lord think they do him service and say, <hi type="italic">Let the Lord be glorified.</hi> But, sooner or later, they will be made to know their error to their cost, to their confusion.
entries.ff37b2e5f8c7e5edca7d05b9ee010e8e8da7e257: <div eID="gen16266" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Sennacherib's Insolent Message. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen16267" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Then said Eliakim and Shebna and Joah unto Rabshakeh, Speak, I pray thee, unto thy servants in the Syrian language; for we understand <hi type="italic">it:</hi> and speak not to us in the Jews' language, in the ears of the people that <hi type="italic">are</hi> on the wall. <hi type="super">12</hi> But Rabshakeh said, Hath my master sent me to thy master and to thee to speak these words? <hi type="italic">hath he</hi> not <hi type="italic">sent me</hi> to the men that sit upon the wall, that they may eat their own dung, and drink their own piss with you? <hi type="super">13</hi> Then Rabshakeh stood, and cried with a loud voice in the Jews' language, and said, Hear ye the words of the great king, the king of Assyria. <hi type="super">14</hi> Thus saith the king, Let not Hezekiah deceive you: for he shall not be able to deliver you. <hi type="super">15</hi> Neither let Hezekiah make you trust in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will surely deliver us: this city shall not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria. <hi type="super">16</hi> Hearken not to Hezekiah: for thus saith the king of Assyria, Make <hi type="italic">an agreement</hi> with me <hi type="italic">by</hi> a present, and come out to me: and eat ye every one of his vine, and every one of his fig tree, and drink ye every one the waters of his own cistern; <hi type="super">17</hi> Until I come and take you away to a land like your own land, a land of corn and wine, a land of bread and vineyards. <hi type="super">18</hi> <hi type="italic">Beware</hi> lest Hezekiah persuade you, saying, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will deliver us. Hath any of the gods of the nations delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria? <hi type="super">19</hi> Where <hi type="italic">are</hi> the gods of Hamath and Arphad? where <hi type="italic">are</hi> the gods of Sepharvaim? and have they delivered Samaria out of my hand? <hi type="super">20</hi> Who <hi type="italic">are they</hi> among all the gods of these lands, that have delivered their land out of my hand, that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand? <hi type="super">21</hi> But they held their peace, and answered him not a word: for the king's commandment was, saying, Answer him not. <hi type="super">22</hi> Then came Eliakim, the son of Hilkiah, that <hi type="italic">was</hi> over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah, the son of Asaph, the recorder, to Hezekiah with <hi type="italic">their</hi> clothes rent, and told him the words of Rabshakeh. <div eID="gen16267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16268" type="x-p"/> We may hence learn these lessons:—1. That, while princes and counsellors have public matters under debate, it is not fair to appeal to the people. It was a reasonable motion which Hezekiah's plenipotentiaries made, that this parley should be held in a language which the people did not understand (<reference osisRef="Isa.36.36">v. 11</reference>), because reasons of state are secret things and ought to be kept secret, the vulgar being incompetent judges of them. It is therefore an unfair practice, and not doing as men would be done by, to incense subjects against their rulers by base insinuations. 2. Proud and haughty scorners, the fairer they are spoken to, commonly speak the fouler. Nothing could be said more mildly and respectfully than that which Hezekiah's agents said to Rabshakeh. Besides that the thing itself was just which they desired, they called themselves his <hi type="italic">servants,</hi> they petitioned for it: <hi type="italic">Speak, we pray thee;</hi> but this made him the more spiteful and imperious. To give rough answers to those who give us soft answers is one way of rendering evil for good; and those are wicked indeed, and it is to be feared incurable, with whom that which usually turns away wrath does but make bad worse. 3. When Satan would tempt men from trusting in God, and cleaving to him, he does so by insinuating that in yielding to him they may better their condition; but it is a false suggestion, and grossly absurd, and therefore to be rejected with the utmost abhorrence. When the world and the flesh say to us, "<hi type="italic">Make an agreement</hi> with us <hi type="italic">and come out to us,</hi> submit to our dominion and come into our interests, and <hi type="italic">you shall eat every one of his own vine,</hi>" they do but deceive us, promising liberty when they would lead us into the basest captivity and slavery. One might as well take Rabshakeh's word as theirs for kind usage and fair quarter; therefore, <hi type="italic">when they speak fair, believe them not.</hi> Let them say what they will, there is no land like the land of promise, the holy land. 4. Nothing can be more absurd in itself, nor a greater affront to the true and living God, than to compare him with the gods of the heathen; as if he could do no more for the protection of his worshippers than they can for the protection of theirs, and as if the God of Israel could as easily be mastered as the gods of Hamath and Arphad, whereas they are vanity and a lie. They are nothing; he is the great <hi type="italic">I AM:</hi> they are the creatures of men's fancy and the works of men's hands; he is the Creator of all things. 5. Presumptuous sinners are ready to think that, because they have been too hard for their fellow-creatures, they are therefore a match for their Creator. This and the other nation they have subdued, and therefore the Lord himself shall not deliver Jerusalem out of their hand. But, though the potsherds may strive with the potsherds of the earth, let them not strive with the potter. 6. It is sometimes prudent not to <hi type="italic">answer a fool according to his folly.</hi> Hezekiah's command was, "<hi type="italic">Answer him not;</hi> it will but provoke him to rail and blaspheme yet more and more; leave it to God to stop his mouth, for you cannot." They had reason enough on their side, but it would be hard to speak it to such an unreasonable adversary without a mixture of passion; and, if they should fall a railing like him, Rabshakeh would be much too hard for them at that weapon. 7. It becomes the people of God to lay to heart the dishonour done to God by the blasphemies of wicked men, though they do not think it prudent to reply to those blasphemies. Though they <hi type="italic">answered him not a word,</hi> yet they rent their clothes, in a holy zeal for the glory of God's name and a holy indignation at the contempt put upon it. They tore their garments when they heard blasphemy, as taking no pleasure in their own ornaments when God's honour suffered.  <chapter eID="Isa.36"/> <div eID="gen16268" type="x-p"/>

entries.59f0331ba7efcf1d386ff0c7e75cd44fd370e5cf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8966"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 36</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.36.1-Isa.36.22">Is 36:1-22</reference>. Sennacherib's Invasion; Blasphemous Solicitations; Hezekiah Is Told of Them.</title> <div sID="gen15082" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">This and the thirty-seventh through thirty-ninth chapters form the historical appendix closing the first division of Isaiah's prophecies, and were added to make the parts of these referring to Assyria more intelligible. So <reference osisRef="Jer.52.1-Jer.52.34">Jr 52:1-34</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.1-2Kgs.25.30">2Ki 25:1-30</reference>. The section occurs almost word for word (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.13">2Ki 18:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.17-2Kgs.18.20">17-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.1-2Kgs.19.37">19:1-37</reference>); <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.14-2Kgs.18.16">2Ki 18:14-16</reference>, however, is additional matter. Hezekiah's "writing" also is in Isaiah, not in Kings (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.9-Isa.38.20">Is 38:9-20</reference>). We know from <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.32">2Ch 32:32</reference> that Isaiah wrote the acts of Hezekiah. It is, therefore, probable, that his record here (Is 36:1-39:8) was incorporated into the Book of Kings by its compiler. Sennacherib lived, according to Assyrian inscriptions, more than twenty years after his invasion; but as Isaiah survived Hezekiah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.32">2Ch 32:32</reference>), who lived upwards of fifteen years after the invasion (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.5">Is 38:5</reference>), the record of Sennacherib's death (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.38">Is 37:38</reference>) is no objection to this section having come from Isaiah; <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.1-2Chr.32.33">2Ch 32:1-33</reference> is probably an abstract drawn from Isaiah's account, as the chronicler himself implies (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.32">2Ch 32:32</reference>). Pul was probably the last of the old dynasty, and Sargon, a powerful satrap, who contrived to possess himself of supreme power and found a new dynasty (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.20.1">Is 20:1</reference>). No attempt was made by Judah to throw off the Assyrian yoke during his vigorous reign. The accession of his son Sennacherib was thought by Hezekiah the opportune time to refuse the long-paid tribute; Egypt and Ethiopia, to secure an ally against Assyria on their Asiatic frontier, promised help; Isaiah, while opposed to submission to Assyria, advised reliance on Jehovah, and not on Egypt, but his advice was disregarded, and so Sennacherib invaded Judea, 712 B.C. He was the builder of the largest of the excavated palaces, that of Koyunjik. Hincks has deciphered his name in the inscriptions. In the third year of his reign, these state that he overran Syria, took Sidon and other Phoenician cities, and then passed to southwest Palestine, where he defeated the Egyptians and Ethiopians (compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.21">2Ki 18:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.9">19:9</reference>). His subsequent retreat, after his host was destroyed by God, is of course suppressed in the inscriptions. But other particulars inscribed agree strikingly with the Bible; the capture of the "defensed cities of Judah," the devastation of the country and deportation of its inhabitants; the increased tribute imposed on Hezekiah--</hi>thirty talents of gold--this exact number being given in both; the silver is set down in the inscriptions at eight hundred talents, in the Bible three hundred; the latter may have been the actual amount carried off, the larger sum may include the silver from the temple doors, pillars, &c. (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.16">2Ki 18:16</reference>).<div eID="gen15082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15083" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8966"/><hi type="bold">1. fourteenth--</hi>the third of Sennacherib's reign. His ultimate object was Egypt, Hezekiah's ally. Hence he, with the great body of his army (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.9">2Ch 32:9</reference>), advanced towards the Egyptian frontier, in southwest Palestine, and did not approach Jerusalem. <div eID="gen15083" type="x-p"/>
entries.26bb19f72a4aae1a8771c6393aa60819abef16cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8967"/><div sID="gen15084" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8967"/><hi type="bold">2. Rab-shakeh--</hi>In <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.17">2Ki 18:17</reference>, Tartan and Rab-saris are joined with him. Rab-shakeh was probably the chief leader; Rab is a title of authority, "chief-cup-bearer."<div eID="gen15084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15085" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lachish--</hi>a frontier town southwest of Jerusalem, in Judah; represented as a great fortified city in a hilly and fruitful country in the Koyunjik bas-reliefs, now in the British Museum; also, its name is found on a slab over a figure of Sennacherib on his throne.<div eID="gen15085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15086" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upper pool--</hi>the side on which the Assyrians would approach Jerusalem coming from the southwest (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.7.3">Is 7:3</reference>). <div eID="gen15086" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c385b196d6e3f9cfb5c2b4eb696a578c0007779: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8968"/><div sID="gen15087" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8968"/><hi type="bold">3. Eliakim--</hi>successor to Shebna, who had been "over the household," that is, chief minister of the king; in <reference osisRef="Isa.22.15-Isa.22.20">Is 22:15-20</reference>, this was foretold.<div eID="gen15087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15088" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scribe--</hi>secretary, recorder--literally, "one who reminds"; a remembrancer to keep the king informed on important facts, and to act as historiographer. In <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.18">2Ki 18:18</reference>, the additional fact is given that the Assyrian envoys "called to the king," in consequence of which Eliakim, &c., "came out to them." <div eID="gen15088" type="x-p"/>
entries.2ce3328f3c89950915bd1a0463e89fb93959eb0e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8969"/><div sID="gen15089" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8969"/><hi type="bold">4. great king--</hi>the usual title of the Persian and Assyrian kings, as they had many subordinate princes or kings under them over provinces (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.8">Is 10:8</reference>). <div eID="gen15089" type="x-p"/>
entries.0a0b3eb47ed5d49698e3ff34928971a61634b116: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8970"/><div sID="gen15090" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8970"/><hi type="bold">5. counsel--</hi>Egypt was famed for its wisdom. <div eID="gen15090" type="x-p"/>
entries.5aa462c0ba0948bbf646e2f31b6d3bf9fe33b64f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8971"/><div sID="gen15091" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8971"/>6. It was a similar alliance with So (that is, Sabacho, or else Sevechus), the Ethiopian king of Egypt, which provoked the Assyrian to invade and destroy Israel, the northern kingdom, under Hoshea. <div eID="gen15091" type="x-p"/>
entries.efca9f4303c8995e2a9808d3fbfa09dd6d0b9a7b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8972"/><div sID="gen15092" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8972"/>7. The Assyrian mistakes Hezekiah's religious reforms whereby he took away the high places (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.4">2Ki 18:4</reference>) as directed against Jehovah. Some of the high places may have been dedicated to Jehovah, but worshipped under the form of an image in violation of the second commandment: the "brazen serpent," also (broken in pieces by Hezekiah, and called Nehushtan, "a piece of brass," because it was worshipped by Israel) was originally set up by God's command. Hence the Assyrian's allegation has a specious color: you cannot look for help from Jehovah, for your king has "taken away His altars."<div eID="gen15092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15093" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to Jerusalem--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.12.5">De 12:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.12.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.4.20">Joh 4:20</reference>). <div eID="gen15093" type="x-p"/>
entries.3f287db5e787a0ee13a79f2b2aeaaebb43476106: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8973"/><div sID="gen15094" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8973"/><hi type="bold">8. give pledges--</hi>a taunting challenge. Only give the guarantee that you can supply as many as two thousand riders, and I will give thee two thousand horses. But seeing that you have not even this small number (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.2.7">Is 2:7</reference>), how can you stand against the hosts of Assyrian cavalry? The Jews tried to supply their weakness in this "arm" from Egypt (<reference osisRef="Isa.31.1">Is 31:1</reference>). <div eID="gen15094" type="x-p"/>
entries.fc375b8b058a1dd2fc5e407570b20d4bbd8ce9b1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8974"/><div sID="gen15095" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8974"/><hi type="bold">9. captain--</hi>a governor under a satrap; even he commands more horsemen than this. <div eID="gen15095" type="x-p"/>
entries.6504ddc72e1fe4ff199b7d245f04918f9f8e6513: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8975"/><div sID="gen15096" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8975"/>10. A boastful inference from the past successes of Assyria, designed to influence the Jews to surrender; their own principles bound them to yield to Jehovah's will. He may have heard from partisans in Judah what Isaiah had foretold (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">Is 10:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.6">6</reference>). <div eID="gen15096" type="x-p"/>
entries.0298059659c321f7fbc535f1d0df5bb0a2d067ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8976"/><div sID="gen15097" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8976"/><hi type="bold">11. Syrian--</hi>rather, "Aramean": the language spoken north and east of Palestine, and understood by the Assyrians as belonging to the same family of languages as their own: nearly akin to Hebrew also, though not intelligible to the multitude (compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.5-2Kgs.5.7">2Ki 5:5-7</reference>). "Aram" means a "high land," and includes parts of Assyria as well as Syria.<div eID="gen15097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15098" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jews' language--</hi>The men of Judah since the disruption of Israel, claimed the Hebrew as their own peculiarly, as if they were now the only true representatives of the whole Hebrew twelve tribes.<div eID="gen15098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15099" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ears of ... people on ... wall--</hi>The interview is within hearing distance of the city. The people crowd on the wall, curious to hear the Assyrian message. The Jewish rulers fear that it will terrify the people and therefore beg Rab-shakeh to speak Aramean. <div eID="gen15099" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce2a38198312304b462855511b88e0471eacdf71: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8977"/><div sID="gen15100" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8977"/>12. Is it to thy master and thee that I am sent? Nay, it is to the men on the wall, to let them know (so far am I from wishing them not to hear, as you would wish), that unless they surrender, they shall be reduced to the direst extremities of famine in the siege (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.11">2Ch 32:11</reference>, explains the word here), namely, to eat their own excrements: or, connecting, "that they may eat," &c., with "sit upon the wall"; who, as they hold the wall, are knowingly exposing themselves to the direst extremities [Maurer]. Isaiah, as a faithful historian, records the filthy and blasphemous language of the Assyrians to mark aright the true character of the attack on Jerusalem. <div eID="gen15100" type="x-p"/>
entries.c07e1d9619e8efb6b7016768f9651e2e6ea795f7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8978"/><div sID="gen15101" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8978"/>13. Rab-shakeh speaks louder and plainer than ever to the men on the wall. <div eID="gen15101" type="x-p"/>
entries.fcd725f435d5ffb60a5a1b38a52f615ca935c896: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8979"/><div sID="gen15102" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8979"/>15. The foes of God's people cannot succeed against them, unless they can shake their trust in Him (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.36.10">Is 36:10</reference>). <div eID="gen15102" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc23a50b334a9c6fe3f7a9fcf374d89560405c66: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8980"/><div sID="gen15103" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8980"/><hi type="bold">16. agreement ... by ... present--</hi>rather, "make peace with me"; literally, "blessing" so called from the mutual congratulations attending the ratification of peace. So Chaldee. Or else, "Do homage to me" [Horsley].<div eID="gen15103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15104" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come out--</hi>surrender to me; then you may remain in quiet possession of your lands till my return from Egypt, when I will lead you away to a land fruitful as your own. Rab-shakeh tries to soften, in the eyes of the Jews, the well-known Assyrian policy of weakening the vanquished by deporting them to other lands (<reference osisRef="Gen.47.21">Ge 47:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">2Ki 17:6</reference>). <div eID="gen15104" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ded053015c0e4001b19fa2f492d3d82a1ea72e8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8981"/><div sID="gen15105" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8981"/><hi type="bold">19. Hamath ... Arphad--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.10.9">Is 10:9</reference>).<div eID="gen15105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15106" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Sepharvaim--</hi>literally, "the two scribes"; now Sipphara, on the east of Euphrates, above Babylon. It was a just retribution (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.31">Pr 1:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.19">Jr 2:19</reference>). Israel worshipped the gods of Sepharvaim, and so colonists of Sepharvaim were planted in the land of Israel (thenceforth called Samaria) by the Assyrian conqueror (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.24">2Ki 17:24</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.34">2Ki 18:34</reference>).<div eID="gen15106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15107" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Samaria--</hi>Shalmaneser began the siege against Hoshea, because of his conspiring with So of Egypt (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.4">2Ki 17:4</reference>). Sargon finished it; and, in his palace at Khorsabad, he has mentioned the number of Israelites carried captive--27,280 [G. V. Smith]. <div eID="gen15107" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a3738a6b26d12bce8807fe1b78069e6afaef79a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8982"/><div sID="gen15108" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8982"/>20. (Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.10.11">Is 10:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.19">2Ch 32:19</reference>). Here he contradicts his own assertion (<reference osisRef="Isa.36.10">Is 36:10</reference>), that he had "come up against the land with the Lord." Liars need good memories. He classes Jehovah with the idols of the other lands; nay, thinks Him inferior in proportion as Judah, under His tutelage, was less than the lands under the tutelage of the idols. <div eID="gen15108" type="x-p"/>
entries.7dc487b801d1948914b0fdf70e7ec0d2e1b43c7b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8983"/><div sID="gen15109" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8983"/><hi type="bold">21. not a word--</hi>so as not to enter into a war of words with the blasphemer (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.14">Ex 14:14</reference>; Jude 9). <div eID="gen15109" type="x-p"/>
entries.0830f8894d31cafc9fe09e71934eb3b521b2b878: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8984"/><div sID="gen15110" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8984"/><hi type="bold">22. clothes rent--</hi>in grief and horror at the blasphemy (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.65">Mt 26:65</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.36"/>

entries.8d6b0f4cf6e04ee64d262751a6900076dac3ee01: <div eID="gen27968" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen27969" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27970" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27970" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27969" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27971" type="x-p"/> Sennacherib, king of Assyria, comes against Judah, and takes all the fenced cities, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.1">Isa 36:1</reference>. He afterwards sends a great host against Jerusalem; and his general Rabshakeh delivers an insulting and blasphemous message to Hezekiah, vv. 2-20. Hezekiah and his people are greatly afflicted at the words of Rabshakeh, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.21">Isa 36:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.22">Isa 36:22</reference>. <div eID="gen27971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27972" type="x-p"/> The history of the invasion of Sennacherib, and of the miraculous destruction of his army Which makes the subject of so many of Isaiah's prophecies, is very properly inserted here as affording the best light to many parts of those prophecies, and as almost necessary to introduce the prophecy in the thirty-seventh chapter, being the answer of God to Hezekiah's prayer, which could not be properly understood without it. We find the same narrative in the Second Book of Kings, chaps. 18, 19, 20.; and these chapters of Isaiah, 36, 37, 38, <reference osisRef="Isa.39.1-Isa.39.8">Isa 39:1-8</reference>, for much the greater part, (the account of the sickness of Hezekiah only excepted), are but a different copy of that narration. The difference of the two copies is little more than what has manifestly arisen from the mistakes of transcribers; they mutually correct each other, and most of the mistakes may be perfectly rectified by a collation of the two copies with the assistance of the ancient versions. Some few sentences, or members of sentences, are omitted in this copy of Isaiah, which are found in the other copy in the Book of Kings. Whether these omissions were made by design or mistake may be doubted. - L.
entries.15b77007d6e318e01bf9e8a4376c8e3f692a550c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen27972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27973" type="x-p"/> Then came forth unto him - Before these words the other copy, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.18">2Kgs 18:18</reference>, adds, ויקראו אל המלך vaiyikreu el hammelech, "And they demanded audience of the king."
entries.90d1d408eaf7c0e391d17028e3df098d52171b08: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen27973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27974" type="x-p"/> I say "Thou hast said" - Fourteen MSS. (three ancient) of Kennicott's and De Rossi's have it in the second person, אמרת amarta; and so the other copy, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.20">2Kgs 18:20</reference>. <div eID="gen27974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27975" type="x-p"/> But they are but vain words - דבר שפתים debar sephathayim, a word of the lips. Thou dost talk about counsels, but thou hast none; about strength, but there is none with thee.
entries.9b7a8466111248700244db19ec350605cfcdf340: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen27975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27976" type="x-p"/> The staff of this broken reed - A weakened, faithless ally. <div eID="gen27976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27977" type="x-p"/> On Egypt - The Bodl. MS. adds מלך melech, the king of Egypt; and so perhaps the Chaldee might read. <div eID="gen27977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27978" type="x-p"/> It will go into his hand, and pierce it - Will take subsidy after subsidy, and do nothing for it.
entries.1c107b5ada33d15926a69aa453db1121c81bf13e: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen27978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27979" type="x-p"/> But if thou say "But if ye say" - Two ancient MSS. have תאמרו tomeru in the plural number; so likewise the Septuagint, Chaldee, and the other copy, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.22">2Kgs 18:22</reference>. <div eID="gen27979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27980" type="x-p"/> Ye shall worship before this altar "To worship only before this altar" - See <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.12">2Chr 32:12</reference>.
entries.2f7601631c5bd2fa2a1d43f71df4c10451b1894f: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen27980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27981" type="x-p"/> Am I now come up without the Lord - Probably some apostate Israelitish priest might have encouraged the king of Assyria by telling him that Jehovah had given him a commission against Jerusalem.
entries.15e6a27a1c27a8bfa7abee4eb0dfd3a1dc69a4c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen27981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27982" type="x-p"/> That they may eat their own dung "Destined to eat their own dung" - לאכל leechol, that they may eat, as our translation literally renders it. But the Syriac reads מאכל meechol, that they may not eat, perhaps rightly, and afterward ומשתות umishshethoth, or ושתות ushethoth, to the same purpose. Seventeen of Dr. Kennicott's MSS., ten of De Rossi's and two of my own, read מימי meymey, the water; mine have מימי שניהם meymey sheneyhem, and write in the margin מימי רגליהם meymey regaleyhem, the water of their feet, a modest way of expressing urine.
entries.4366a566f457a946b958166ea4b6c10ddf2d0176: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen27982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27983" type="x-p"/> This city shall not be delivered - ולא velo, And this city. Ten of Kennicott's MSS., and nine of De Rossi's, with one (ancient) of my own, add the conjunction.
entries.47ebfce471a84ce2bb96b27138f583eec8a6d5d9: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen27983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27984" type="x-p"/> Make an agreement - ברכה berachah, make a blessing with me; i.e., Give me a ransom for the city, and I will not destroy it; give me the yearly tribute thou hast promised.
entries.cd5a80525b10033c0d355bdad9424ea70f8bcb7d: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen27984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27985" type="x-p"/> And vineyards - The other copy, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.32">2Kgs 18:32</reference>, adds here: "A land of oil-olive, and of honey; that ye may live, and not die: and hearken not unto Hezekiah when he seduceth you."
entries.a63fc4eb5db28b3e2dcfdb1fba95e45f588a57db: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen27985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27986" type="x-p"/> Where are the gods - Many MSS. add the conjunction here also: And, or But, where are the gods, etc. <div eID="gen27986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27987" type="x-p"/> For other matters relative to this chapter, see the notes on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.13">2Kgs 18:13</reference> (note), etc. <div eID="gen27987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27988" type="x-p"/> Of Sepharvaim - The other copy, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.34">2Kgs 18:34</reference>, adds, of "Henah and Ivah." <div eID="gen27988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27989" type="x-p"/> Have they delivered - וכי vechi. The copulative is not expressed here by the Septuagint, Syriac, Vulgate, and three MSS.; nor is it in any other copy. Ib. Houbigant reads הכי hachi, with the interrogative particle; a probable conjecture, which the ancient Versions above quoted seem to favor.
entries.a365e89a1bdbbd295b9f3bfd7e2ba4e1fce7ffc1: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen27989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27990" type="x-p"/> But they held their peace "But the people held their peace" - The word העם haam, the people, is supplied from the other copy, and is authorized by a MS. which inserts it after אתו otho.  <chapter eID="Isa.36"/> <div eID="gen27990" type="x-p"/>

entries.9c3b8ac938b11b790d5ee139f31ef061fe3fd042: <reference osisRef="Isa.36.1-Isa.36.2">Isa 36:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen13250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13251" type="x-p"/> Marcus V. Niebuhr, in his <hi type="italic">History of Asshur and Babel</hi> (p. 164), says, “Why should not Hezekiah have revolted from Asshur as soon as he ascended the throne? He had a motive for doing this, which other kings had not - namely, that as he held his kingdom in fief from his God, obedience to a temporal monarch was in his case sin.” But this assumption, which is founded upon the same idea as that in which the question was put to Jesus concerning the tribute money, is not at all in accordance with Isaiah’s view, as we may see from chapters 28-32; and Hezekiah’s revolt cannot have occurred even in the sixth year of his reign. For Shalmanassar, or rather Sargon, made war upon Egypt and Ethiopia after the destruction of Samaria (<reference osisRef="Isa.20.1-Isa.20.6">Isa 20:1-6</reference>; cf., Oppert, <hi type="italic">Les Inscriptions des Sargonides</hi>, pp. 22, 27), without attempting anything against Hezekiah. It was not till the time of Sargon, who overthrew the reigning house of Assyria, that the actual preparations for the revolt were commenced, by the formation of an alliance between the kingdom of Judah on the one hand, and Egypt, and probably Philistia, on the other, the object of which was the rupture of the Assyrian yoke.<note placement="foot">The name <hi type="italic">Amgarron</hi> upon the earthenware prism of Sennacherib does not mean <hi type="italic">Migron</hi> (Oppert), but <hi type="italic">Ekron</hi> (Rawlinson).</note> <div eID="gen13251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13252" type="x-p"/> The campaign of Sennacherib the son of Sargon, into which we are transported in the following history, was the third of his expeditions, the one to which Sennacherib himself refers in the inscription upon the prism: “<hi type="italic">dans ma ̄e campagne je marchai vers la Syrie</hi>.” The position which we find Sennacherib taking up between Philistia and Jerusalem, to the south-west of the latter, is a very characteristic one in relation to both the occasion and the ultimate object of the campaign.<note placement="foot">We shall show the variations in the text of 2Ki 18:13., as far as we possibly can, in our translation. K. signifies the book of Kings. But the task of pronouncing an infallible sentence upon them all we shall leave to those who know everything.</note> <div eID="gen13252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13253" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.1">Isa 32:1</reference> <hi type="italic">“And it came to pass in the</hi> (K.<hi type="italic">and in the</hi>)<hi type="italic">fourteenth year of king Hizkîyahu, Sancherîb king of Asshur came up against all the fortified cities of Judah, and took them. </hi>(K. adds:<hi type="italic">Then Hizkiyah king of Judah sent to the king of Asshur to Lachish, saying, I have sinned, withdraw from me again; what thou imposest upon me I will raise. And the king of Asshur imposed upon Hizkiyah king of Judah three hundred talents of silver, and thirty talents of gold. And Hizkiyah gave up all the silver that was in the house of Jehovah, and in the treasures of the king’s house. At the same time Hizkiyah mutilated the doors of the temple of Jehovah, and the pillars which Hizkiyah king of Judah had plated with gold, and gave it to the king of Asshur</hi>)<hi type="italic">.”</hi> This long addition, which is distinguished at once by the introduction of חזיקה in the place of חזקיהו, is probably only an annalistic interpolation, though one of great importance in relation to Isa 33:7. What follows in Isaiah does not dovetail well into this addition, and therefore does not presuppose its existence. <reference osisRef="Isa.36.2">Isa 36:2</reference> <hi type="italic">“Then the king of Asshur sent Rabshakeh </hi>(K.:<hi type="italic">Tartan, and Rabsaris, and Rabshakeh</hi>)<hi type="italic">from Lachish towards Jerusalem to king Hizkiyahu with a great army, and he advanced </hi>(K.:<hi type="italic">to king H. with a great army to Jerusalem; and they went up and came to Jerusalem, and went up, and came and advanced</hi>)<hi type="italic">to the conduit of the upper pool by the road of the fuller’s field.”</hi> Whereas in K. the repeated ויבאו ויעלו (and went up and came) forms a “dittography,” the names <hi type="italic">Tartan</hi> and <hi type="italic">Rab-saris</hi> have apparently dropped out of the text of Isaiah, as <reference osisRef="Isa.37.6">Isa 37:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.24">Isa 37:24</reference> presuppose a plurality of messengers. The three names are not names of persons, but official titles, viz., the commander-in-chief (<hi type="italic">Tartan</hi>, which really occurs in an Assyrian list of offices; see Rawlinson, <hi type="italic">Monarchies</hi>, ii. 412), the chief cup-bearer (רבשׁקה with <hi type="italic">tzere</hi> = רבשׁקא)). The situation of <hi type="italic">Lachish</hi> is marked by the present ruins of <hi type="italic">Umm Lakis</hi>, to the south-west of <hi type="italic">Bet-Gibrin</hi> ((Eleutheropolis) in the Shephelah. The messengers come from the south-west with the <hi type="italic">ultima ratio</hi> of a strong detachment (חיל a connecting form, from חיל, like גדולה גּיא, Zec 14:4; Ewald, §287,<hi type="italic">a</hi>); they therefore halt on the western side of Jerusalem (on the locality, see at <reference osisRef="Isa.7.3">Isa 7:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.8-Isa.22.11">Isa 22:8-11</reference>; compare Keil on Kings).
entries.f4b409897b4d45c710df7dfef09627cd59fc4011: <reference osisRef="Isa.36.3-Isa.36.10">Isa 36:3-10</reference> <div eID="gen13253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13254" type="x-p"/> Hezekiah’s confidential ministers go there also. <reference osisRef="Isa.36.3">Isa 36:3</reference> (K. <hi type="italic">“And they called to the king</hi>)<hi type="italic">, and there went out to him </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">to them</hi>)<hi type="italic">Eliakim son of Hilkiyahu, the house-minister, and Shebna the chancellor, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder.”</hi> On the office of the house-minister, or major-domo, which was now filled by Eliakim instead of Shebna (שׁבנא, K. twice שׁבנה), see Isa 22:15.; and on that of <hi type="italic">sōphēr</hi> and <hi type="italic">mazkı̄r</hi>. Rabshakeh’s message follows in <reference osisRef="Isa.36.4-Isa.36.10">Isa 36:4-10</reference> :<hi type="italic">“And Rabshakeh said to them, Say now to Hizkiyahu, Thus saith the great king, the king of Asshur, What sort of confidence is this that thou hast got? I say </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">thou sayest, i.e., thou talkest</hi>),<hi type="italic">vain talk is counsel and strength for war: now, then, in whom dost thou trust, that thou hast rebelled against me? </hi>(K. <hi type="italic">Now</hi>)<hi type="italic">Behold, thou trustest </hi>(K. לּך)<hi type="italic">in this broken reed-staff there, in Egypt, on which one leans, and it runs into his hand and pierces it; so does Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him. But if thou sayest to me </hi>(K. <hi type="italic">ye say</hi>),<hi type="italic">We trust in Jehovah our God; is it not He whose high places and altars Hizkiyahu has removed, and has said to Judah and Jerusalem, Ye shall worship before the altar </hi>(K. ads,<hi type="italic">in Jerusalem</hi>)?<hi type="italic">And now take a wager with my lord </hi>(K. <hi type="italic">with</hi>) <hi type="italic">the king of Asshur; I will deliver thee two thousand horses, if thou art able for thy part to give horsemen upon them. And how couldst thou repel the advance of a single satrap among the least of the servants of my lord?! Thou puttest thy trust then in Egypt for chariots and riders! And </hi>(omitted in K.)<hi type="italic">now have I come up without Jehovah against this land to destroy it </hi>(K. <hi type="italic">against this place, to destroy it</hi>)?<hi type="italic">Jehovah said to me, Go up to </hi>(K. against)<hi type="italic">this land, and destroy it.”</hi> The chronicler has a portion of this address of Rabshakeh in <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.10">2Ch 32:10</reference>-12. And just as the prophetic words in the book of Kings have a Deuteronomic sound, and those in the Chronicles the ring of a chronicle, so do Rabshakeh’s words, and those which follow, sound like the words of Isaiah himself. “The great king” is the standing royal title appended to the names of Sargon and Sennacherib upon the Assyrian monuments (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.10.8">Isa 10:8</reference>). Hezekiah is not thought worthy of the title of king, ether here or afterwards. The reading אמרתּ in <reference osisRef="Isa.36.5">Isa 36:5</reference> (thou speakest vain talk) is not the preferable one, because in that case we should expect דּבּרתּ, or rather (according to the usual style) אך דּבּרתּ. The meaning is, that he must look upon Hezekiah’s resolution, and his strength (וּגבוּרה עצה connected as in <reference osisRef="Isa.11.2">Isa 11:2</reference>) for going to war, as mere boasting (“lip-words,” as in <reference osisRef="Prov.14.23">Pro 14:23</reference>), and must therefore assume that there was something in the background of which he was well aware. And this must be Egypt, which would not only be of no real help to its ally, but would rather do him harm by leaving him in the lurch. The figure of a reed-staff has been borrowed by Ezekiel in <reference osisRef="Isa.29.6">Isa 29:6</reference>-7. It was a very appropriate one for Egypt, with its abundance of reeds and rushes (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.6">Isa 19:6</reference>), and it has Isaiah’s peculiar ring (for the expression itself, compare <reference osisRef="Isa.42.3">Isa 42:3</reference>; and for the fact itself, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.5">Isa 30:5</reference>, and other passages). רצוּץ does not mean fragile (Luzz. <hi type="italic">quella fragil canna</hi>), but broken, namely, in consequence of the loss of the throne by the native royal family, from whom it had been wrested by the Ethiopians (<reference osisRef="Isa.18.1-Isa.18.7">Isa 18:1-7</reference>), and the defeats sustained at the hands of Sargon (<reference osisRef="Isa.20.1-Isa.20.6">Isa 20:1-6</reference>). The construction <hi type="italic">cui quis innitur et intrat is paratactic for cui si quis</hi>. In <reference osisRef="Isa.36.7">Isa 36:7</reference> the reading תאמרוּן commends itself, from the fact that the sentence is not continued with הסירת; but as Hezekiah is addressed throughout, and it is to him that the reply is to be made, the original reading was probably תאמר. The fact that Hezekiah had restricted the worship of Jehovah to Jerusalem, by removing the other places of worship (2Ki 18:4), is brought against him in a thoroughly heathen, and yet at the same time (considering the inclination to worship other gods which still existed in the nation) a very crafty manner. In <reference osisRef="Isa.36.8">Isa 36:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.9">Isa 36:9</reference>, he throws in his teeth, with most imposing scorn, his own weakness as compared with Asshur, which was chiefly dreaded on account of its strength in cavalry and war-chariots. נא התערב does not refer to the performance and counter-performance which follow, in the sense of “connect thyself” (Luzz. <hi type="italic">associati</hi>), but is used in a similar sense to the Omeric μιγῆναι, though with the idea of vying with one another, not of engaging in war (the synonym in the Talmud is <hi type="italic">himrâh</hi>, to bet, e.g., <hi type="italic">b. Sabbath</hi> 31 <hi type="italic">a</hi>): a bet and a pledge are kindred notions (Heb. ערבון, cf., Lat. <hi type="italic">vadari</hi>). On <hi type="italic">pechâh</hi> (for <hi type="italic">pachâh</hi>), which also occurs as an Assyrian title in <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.6">Eze 23:6</reference>, Eze 23:23. אחד פּחת, two constructives, the first of which is to be explained according to Ewald, §286, a (compare above, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.2">Isa 36:2</reference>, כבד חיל), form the logical <hi type="italic">regens</hi> of the following <hi type="italic">servorum dominin mei minimorum</hi>; and <hi type="italic">hēshı̄bh penē</hi> does not mean here to refuse a petitioner, but to repel an antagonist (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.6">Isa 28:6</reference>). The <hi type="italic">fut. consec.</hi> ותּבטח deduces a consequence: Hezekiah could not do anything by himself, and therefore he trusted in Egypt, from which he expected chariots and horsemen. In <reference osisRef="Isa.36.10">Isa 36:10</reference>, the prophetic idea, that Asshur was the instrument employed by Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">Isa 10:5</reference>, etc.), is put into the mouth of the Assyrian himself. This is very conceivable, but the colouring of Isaiah is undeniable.
entries.a44ba7b4cee2b074b1053e4afa0331e1f05f4d1c: <reference osisRef="Isa.36.11">Isa 36:11</reference> <div eID="gen13254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13255" type="x-p"/> The concluding words, in which the Assyrian boasts of having Jehovah on his side, affect the messengers of Hezekiah in the keenest manner, especially because of the people present. <hi type="italic">“Then said Eliakim </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">the son of Hilkiyahu</hi>)<hi type="italic">, and Shebna, and Joah, to Rabshakeh, Pray, speak to thy servants in Aramaean, for we understand it; and do not speak to </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">with</hi>)<hi type="italic">us in Jewish, in the ears of the people that are on the wall.”</hi> They spoke <hi type="italic">Yehūdı̄th</hi>, i.e., the colloquial language of the kingdom of Judah. The kingdom of Israel was no longer in existence, and the language of the Israelitish nation, as a whole, might therefore already be called Judaean (Jewish), as in <reference osisRef="Neh.13.24">Neh 13:24</reference>, more especially as there may have been a far greater dialectical difference between the popular speech of the northern and southern kingdoms, than we can gather from the biblical books that were written in the one or the other. Aramaean (<hi type="italic">'arâmı̄th</hi>), however, appears to have been even then, as it was at a later period (Ezr 4:7), the language of intercourse between the empire of Eastern Asia and the people to the west of the Tigris (compare Alex. Polyhistor in Euseb. <hi type="italic">chron. arm.</hi> i. 43, where Sennacherib is said to have erected a monument with a Chaldean inscription); and consequently educated Judaeans not only understood it, but were able to speak it, more especially those who were in the service of the state. Assyrian, on the contrary, was unintelligible to Judaeans (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.11">Isa 28:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.19">Isa 33:19</reference>), although this applied comparatively less to the true Assyrian dialect, which was Semitic, and can be interpreted for the most part from the Hebrew (see Oppert’s “Outlines of an Assyrian Grammar” in the <hi type="italic">Journal Asiatique</hi>, 1859), than to the motley language of the Assyrian army, which was a compound of Arian and Turanian elements. The name Sennacherib (<hi type="italic">Sanchērı̄bh</hi> = סן־אסהי־ירב, lxx <hi type="italic">Sennachēreim</hi>, i.e., “Sin, the moon-god, had multiplied the brethren”) is Semitic; on the other hand, the name Tartan, which cannot be interpreted either from the Semitic or the Arian, is an example of the element referred to, which was so utterly strange to a Judaean ear.
entries.58505222367c921bae0891999810586270565917: <reference osisRef="Isa.36.12">Isa 36:12</reference> <div eID="gen13255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13256" type="x-p"/> The harsh reply is given in Isa 36:12. <hi type="italic">“Then Rabshakeh said </hi>(K. <hi type="italic">to them</hi>),<hi type="italic">Has my lord sent me to </hi>(K. העל)<hi type="italic">the men who sit upon the wall, to eat their dung, and to drink their urine together with you?”</hi> - namely, because their rulers were exposing them to a siege which would involve the most dreadful state of famine.
entries.c657f3499bb4d3365dc2725f3464533108e98ef7: <reference osisRef="Isa.36.13-Isa.36.20">Isa 36:13-20</reference> <div eID="gen13256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13257" type="x-p"/> After Rabshakeh had refused the request of Hezekiah’s representatives in this contemptuous manner, he turned in defiance of them to the people themselves. <hi type="italic">“Then Rabshakeh went near, and cried with a loud voice in the Jewish language </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">and spake</hi>)<hi type="italic">, and said, Hear the words</hi> (K.<hi type="italic">the word</hi>)<hi type="italic">of the great king, the king of Asshur. Thus saith the king, Let not Hizkiyahu practise deception upon you </hi>(יסה<hi type="italic">, </hi> K.יסהיא))<hi type="italic">; for he cannot deliver you </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">out of his hand</hi>)<hi type="italic">. And let not Hizkiyahu feed you with hope in Jehovah, saying, Jehovah will deliver, yea, deliver us: </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">and</hi>)<hi type="italic">this city will not be delivered into the hand of the king of Asshur. Hearken not to Hizkiyahu: for thus saith the king </hi>(<hi type="italic">hammelekh ,</hi> K.<hi type="italic">melekh</hi>)<hi type="italic">of Asshur, Enter into a connection of mutual good wishes with me, and come out to me: and enjoy every one his vine, and every one his fig-tree, and drink every one the water of his cistern; till I come and take you away into a land like your land, a land of corn and wine, a land of bread-corn and vineyards </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">a land full of fine olive-trees and honey, and live and do not die, and hearken not to Hizkiyahu</hi>)<hi type="italic">; that Hizkiyahu to not befool you </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">for he befools you</hi>)<hi type="italic">, saying, Jehovah will deliver us! Have the gods of the nations delivered </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">really delivered</hi>)<hi type="italic">every one his land out of the hand of the king of Asshur? Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? where the gods of Sepharvayim </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">adds, Hena‛ and ‛Ivah</hi>)<hi type="italic">? and how much less </hi>(וכי, K. כּי)<hi type="italic">have they delivered that Samaria out of my hand? Who were they among all the gods of these </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">of the</hi>)<hi type="italic">lands, who delivered their land out of my hand? how much less will Jehovah deliver Jerusalem out of my hand!?</hi> The chronicler also has this continuation of Rabshakeh’s address in part (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.13-2Chr.32.15">2Ch 32:13-15</reference>), but he has fused into one the Assyrian self-praise uttered by Rabshakeh on his first and second mission. The encouragement of the people, by referring to the help of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.6-2Chr.32.8">2Ch 32:6-8</reference>), is placed by him before this first account is given by Isaiah, and forms a conclusion to the preparations for the contest with Asshur as there described. Rabshakeh now draws nearer to the wall, and harangues the people. השּׁיא is construed here with a dative (to excite treacherous hopes); whereas in <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.15">2Ch 32:15</reference> it is written with an accusative. The reading מיּדו is altered from מיּדי in <reference osisRef="Isa.36.20">Isa 36:20</reference>, which is inserted still more frequently by the chronicler. The reading את־העיר with תנּתן is incorrect; it would require ינּתן (Ges. §143, 1 <hi type="italic">a</hi>). To make a <hi type="italic">berâkhâh</hi> with a person was equivalent to entering into a relation of blessing, i.e., into a state of mind in which each wished all prosperity to the other. This was probably a common phrase, though we only meet with it here. יצא, when applied to the besieged, is equivalent to surrendering (e.g., <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.3">1Sa 11:3</reference>). If they did that, they should remain in quiet possession and enjoyment, until the Assyrian fetched them away (after the Egyptian campaign was over), and transported them to a land which he describes to them in the most enticing terms, in order to soften down the inevitable transportation. It is a question whether the expansion of this picture in the book of Kings is original or not; since ועוּה הנע in <reference osisRef="Isa.36.19">Isa 36:19</reference> appears to be also tacked on here from <reference osisRef="Isa.37.13">Isa 37:13</reference> (see at this passage). On <hi type="italic">Hamath</hi> and <hi type="italic">Arpad</hi> (to the north of Haleb in northern Syria, and a different place from <hi type="italic">Arvad</hi> = <hi type="italic">Arad</hi>), see Isa 10:9. <hi type="italic">Sepharvayim</hi> (a dual form, the house of the <hi type="italic">Sepharvı̄m</hi>, 2Ki 17:31) is the Sipphara of Ptol. v. 18, 7, the southernmost city of Mesopotamia, on the left bank of the Euphrates; Pliny’s <hi type="italic">Hipparenum</hi> on the <hi type="italic">Narraga</hi>, i.e., the canal, <hi type="italic">nehar malkâ</hi>, the key to the irrigating or inundating works of Babylon, which were completed afterwards by Nebuchadnezzar (Plin. <hi type="italic">h. n.</hi> vi. 30); probably the same place as the sun-city, <hi type="italic">Sippara</hi>, in which Xisuthros concealed the sacred books before the great flood (see K. Müller’s <hi type="italic">Fragmenta Historicorum Gr.</hi> ii. 501-2). פּן in <reference osisRef="Isa.36.18">Isa 36:18</reference> has a warning meaning (as if it followed לכם השּׁמרו   ); and both וכי and כּי in <reference osisRef="Isa.36.19">Isa 36:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.20">Isa 36:20</reference>, introduce an exclamatory clause when following a negative interrogatory sentence: and that they should have saved,” or “that Jehovah should save,” equivalent to “how much less have they saved, or will He save” (Ewald, §354, c; comp. אף־כּי,   <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.15">2Ch 32:15</reference>). Rabshakeh’s words in <reference osisRef="Isa.36.18-Isa.36.20">Isa 36:18-20</reference> are the same as those in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.8">Isa 10:8</reference>-11. The manner in which he defies the gods of the heathen, of Samaria, and last of all of Jerusalem, corresponds to the prophecy there. It is the prophet himself who acts as historian here, and describes the fulfilment of the prophecy, though without therefore doing violence to his character as a prophet.
entries.50af212c9a68ba13610e76603de4b0fba010d46f: <reference osisRef="Isa.36.21-Isa.36.22">Isa 36:21-22</reference> <div eID="gen13257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13258" type="x-p"/> The effect of Rabshakeh’s words. <hi type="italic">“But they held their peace </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">and they, the people, held their peace</hi>)<hi type="italic">, and answered him not a word; for it was the king’s commandment, saying, Ye shall not answer him. Then came Eliakim son of Hilkiyahu </hi>(K.<hi type="italic">Hilkiyah</hi>)<hi type="italic">, the house-minister, and Shebna the chancellor, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder, to Hizkiyahu, with torn clothes, and told him the words of Rabshakeh.”</hi> It is only a superficial observation that could commend the reading in Kings, “They, the people, held their peace,” which Hitzig and Knobel prefer, but which Luzzatto very properly rejects. As the Assyrians wished to speak to the king himself (2Ki 18:18), who sent the three to them as his representatives, the command to hear, and to make no reply, can only have applied to them (and they had already made the matter worse by the one remark which they had made concerning the language); and the reading ויּחרישׁוּ in the text of Isaiah is the correct one. The three were silent, because the king had imposed the duty of silence upon them; and regarding themselves as dismissed, inasmuch as Rabshakeh had turned away from them to the people, they hastened to the king, rending their clothes, in despair and grief and the disgrace they had experienced.  <chapter eID="Isa.36"/> <div eID="gen13258" type="x-p"/>

entries.32beda784395f556955ec189ec438c8a3130bcfd: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.36.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.36.1" sID="gen47167" type="section"/> <div sID="gen47168" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi><hi type="italic"> It happened in the fourteenth year. </hi>In this and the following chapter the Prophet relates a remarkable history, which may be regarded as the seal of his doctrine, in which he predicted the calamities that would befall his nation, and at the same time promised that God would be merciful to them, and would drive back the Assyrians and defend Jerusalem and the Holy Land. What had already been accomplished made it evident that he had not spoken in vain; but God intended that it should also be testified to posterity. Yet to the men of that age it was not less advantageous that such a record should be preserved. He had often threatened that the vengeance of God was near at hand, and that the Assyrians were ready at his bidding to be employed by him as scourges; and st the same time he promised that he would assist Jerusalem even when matters were come to the worst. Both were accomplished, and the greater part of the nation passed by, as with closed eyes, those evident judgments of God, and not less basely despised the assistance which was offered to them. So much the more inexcusable was their gross stupidity.<div eID="gen47168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47169" type="x-p"/>But to the small number of believers it was advantageous to perceive such illustrious proofs of the hand of God, that greater credit might afterwards be given to Isaiah. The Prophet also might pursue his course more ardently and with unshaken firmness, since God had given so splendid an attestation of his doctrine from heaven. And because the truth of God scarcely obtains from us the honor due to it, unless it be supported by strong proofs, God has provided not less largely for our weakness, that we may perceive as in a mirror that the power of God accompanied the words of Isaiah, and that what he taught on earth was confirmed from heaven. More especially has calling was manifestly sealed, when God delivered Jerusalem from the grievous siege of Sennacherib, and when no hope of safety remained; so that believers saw that they had been rescued from the jaws of death by the hand of God alone. For this reason I have said that it was a seal to authenticate the prophecies which might otherwise have been called in question.<div eID="gen47169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47170" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">In the fourteenth year. </hi>Not without reason does he specify the time when these things happened; for at that time Hezekiah had restored the worship of God throughout the whole of his dominions, (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.4">2 Kings 18:4</reference>;) and, not satisfied with this, sent messengers in various directions to invite the Israelites to come with speed from every place to Jerusalem, to offer sacrifices, and, after long disunion, again to unite in holy harmony of faith, and to worship God according to the injunctions of the Law. While such was the condition of the kingdom that superstitions were removed and the Temple cleansed, and thus the true worship of God was restored, Judea is invaded by the king of Assyria, fields are pillaged, cities are taken, and the whole country is subject to his authority. Jerusalem alone, with a few inhabitants, is left; and in that city Hezekiah was shut up as in a prison.<div eID="gen47170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47171" type="x-p"/>We must now consider what thoughts might occur to the pious king and to other persons; for if we judge of this calamity according to the perception of the flesh, we shall think that God was unjust in permitting his servant to be reduced to such extremities, whose piety seemed to deserve that the Lord would preserve him in safety and free from all molestation, since his whole desire was to maintain the true worship of God. This was no small trial of the faith of Hezekiah, and ought to be continually placed before our eyes, when we are subjected to the same temptations. The Lord did not punish Hezekiah for carelessness, pleasures, or luxury, and much less for superstitions, or unholy contempt of the Law; for as soon as he began to reign, he labored with the utmost zeal and carefulness and industry to restore the purity of religion. God therefore intended to try his faith and patience.<div eID="gen47171" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.36.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen47167" osisID="Isa.36.1" type="section"/>
entries.1251906c2712e48aa0d64d457ed574b1a3ee09c4: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.36.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.36.2" sID="gen47172" type="section"/> <div sID="gen47173" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi><hi type="italic"> Then the king of Assyria Rent Rabshakeh. </hi>The order of the narrative may here have been altered; for he had formerly said that Sennacherib had taken all the cities of Judea, and now he says that he sent Rabshakeh <note n="28"> <div sID="gen47174" type="x-p"/> “The Hebrew doctors will have it that this Rabshakeh was an apostate Jew, and Procopius is of the same opinion, which is not altogether improbable, both because he could speak readily in the Hebrew tongue, and when he blasphemed the Divine Majesty, the king and nobles rent their clothes, which was not usual unless he that uttered such blasphemous words was an Israelite. Some think his name imports that he was the principal cupbearer to the king of Assyria, who assumed to himself the title of the Great King, because of his great conquests and large dominions.” — <hi type="italic">White.</hi><div eID="gen47174" type="x-p"/> </note> from Lachish, implying that he was besieging it, and consequently he had not yet stormed them all. But it ought to be observed that historical connection is frequently disturbed, and that what was first in the order of time, comes last in the narrative. Besides, the Scriptures frequently make use of a figure of speech in which a part is taken for the whole, and by which it might be said that all the cities were taken, because those which had been left were few, and Hezekiah had no means of intercourse with them. It appeared, therefore, that the king of Assyria had brought the whole of Judea under his dominion, because nearly all that remained was Jerusalem alone, in which Hezekiah was shut up.<div eID="gen47173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47175" type="x-p"/>This history is more fully related in the Books of Kings, where it is shewn how eager for peace Hezekiah was; for he labored to obtain it on any terms. He had delivered up “three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold,” which that tyrant had demanded; and he found it necessary to seize the vessels of the Temple, and the golden plates which had been attached to its doors, to make up that sum, because his treasury was exhausted. (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.14">2 Kings 18:14</reference>.) But as such gulfs are insatiable, when he had received that money, he next demanded more, and sought to enforce harder conditions. This was done partly, in order to provoke and torment Hezekiah, (for, having once abused the ready compliance of the pious king, he thought that he would obtain anything,) and partly because he sought an occasion of renewing the war. Yet it ought to be observed that the people were justly punished for their iniquities, as had been foretold; for although true religion flourished as to external worship, yet their life was not changed for the better, and their wickedness was not removed, nor was the inward pollution cleansed from their hearts. Accordingly, because the people did not repent, it was necessary that their obstinate depravity should be severely chastised. But because the measure of their iniquities was not yet full, God abated the fierceness of his anger, and suddenly, when matters were desperate, brought such assistance as could not have been believed.<div eID="gen47175" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.36.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen47172" osisID="Isa.36.2" type="section"/>
entries.dcc163351c42349de420a4300f2052298cde6b5c: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.36.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.36.3" sID="gen47176" type="section"/> <div sID="gen47177" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.</hi><hi type="italic"> And Eliakim went to him. Eliakim </hi>was formerly mentioned. It was he to whom the Lord promised that he would give him the chief power in the kingdom after the banishment of Shebna. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.22.20">Isaiah 22:20</reference>.) It now appears as if that promise had failed, when he is sent to an enemy as a suppliant, and as one who is about to surrender himself and his companions, and to undergo cruel tyranny. This might also fill the hearts of believers with anxiety, and lead them to doubt the promises of God. Besides, the godly king had such a scarcity of good men, that, along with Eliakim, he was compelled to send Shebna, whom he knew well to be deceitful and treacherous.<div eID="gen47177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47178" type="x-p"/><foreign xml:lang="he">ספר</foreign><hi type="italic"> (sopher) </hi>means<hi type="italic"> scribe; </hi>and accordingly it often denotes learned men or doctors, and sometimes those who took charge of writings and those who had the custody of the royal records. I have translated it <hi type="italic">chancellor, </hi>for unquestionably it does not relate to legal skill; and we may infer that this Shebna held a high rank, though he had been deprived of his office as governor. <foreign xml:lang="he"> מזכיר</foreign><hi type="italic">(mazkir) </hi>denotes a secretary or recorder.<div eID="gen47178" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.36.3" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen47176" osisID="Isa.36.3" type="section"/>
entries.6e107d0336363cb1dc9f8c90c54788a618815f96: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.36.4" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.36.4" sID="gen47179" type="section"/> <div sID="gen47180" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4.</hi><hi type="italic"> Say now to Hezekiah. </hi>He relates that the three ambassadors, though they were attended by all the magnificence that yet remained in the kingdom, were not only repulsed, but disdainfully treated by the tyrant’s delegate, and loaded with disgraceful reproaches; for, as if Hezekiah had been convicted of wicked revolt, Rabshakeh asks how he had dared to rebel. The particle <foreign xml:lang="he">נא</foreign> (<hi type="italic">na</hi>) is supposed by some to denote entreaty, and is rendered by them <hi type="italic">I pray; </hi>but it would be unsuitable to a proud and insolent man to entreat in this manner. He speaks in the ordinary language of those who lay conditions on the vanquished, or on those who are overwhelmed with fear, whom they wish to compel to make an unconditional surrender, or, as we commonly say, <hi type="italic">(sommer) to summon.</hi><div eID="gen47180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47181" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Thus saith the great king. </hi>In order to give greater validity to the summons, that general speaks in the name of his king, whose greatness he extols to the skies, in order to terrify Hezekiah, when he learns that he has to do with a king of such vast resources. He does not only mean that the first monarch in the world was far superior to Hezekiah, who in comparison of him was but a petty prince; but he calls the king of Assyria <hi type="italic">great, </hi>because by his power he eclipsed all others, so that he stood alone in his lofty rank. By these thunderbolts of words Hezekiah might have been overthrown and subdued, especially since he was so far from being able to resist the power of that tyrant that he was shut up in the city and unable to move out of it.<div eID="gen47181" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.36.4" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen47179" osisID="Isa.36.4" type="section"/>
entries.581a7ee8b620cd8c98e0d19c7c3361445f2f6fb1: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.36.5" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.36.5" sID="gen47182" type="section"/> <div sID="gen47183" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">5.</hi><hi type="italic"> I have said (only a word of the lips.) </hi>In the sacred history (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.20">2 Kings 18:20</reference>) the word employed is, <hi type="italic">Thou hast said</hi> This may be explained as a declaration what kind of courage Rabshakeh thinks that Hezekiah possesses; as if he had said, “Such are thy deliberations.” In this passage the use of the first person, “I have said,” does not alter the sense; because Rabshakeh, as if he had examined the counsels of Hezekiah and fully understood them all, ironically reproaches him; “I see what thou art thinking, but they are <hi type="italic">words of the lips.” </hi>This passage is explained in various ways. Some interpret it, “Thou sayest, that thou hast not merely words of the lips,” that is, “Thou boastest that thou excellest not only in the use of words, but likewise in courage and wisdom.” Others interpret it, “Thou hast words indeed, but wisdom and courage are necessary in war.”<div eID="gen47183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47184" type="x-p"/>Some think that by “words” are meant “prayers.” I do not approve of that exposition; for it is excessively farfetched and unnatural, and therefore I view it thus: “Hezekiah has words of lips, that is, he employs a beautiful and elegant style, to keep the people in the discharge of their duty, or, as we commonly say, <hi type="italic">He has fine speeches;</hi> <note n="29"> <div sID="gen47185" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="fr">Il a de belles paroles</foreign>.<div eID="gen47185" type="x-p"/> </note> but it is not by these that war can be begun or carried on.” He therefore means, that he perfectly understands what Hezekiah is doing, and what it is on which he places his chief reliance, namely, on words and eloquence; <note n="30"> <div sID="gen47186" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Assavoir, sur belles paroles</foreign>.” “Namely, on fine speeches.”<div eID="gen47186" type="x-p"/> </note> but these are of no use for war, in which wisdom and courage are needed. It might also be appropriately viewed as relating to the Egyptians, as if he had said that Hezekiah acts foolishly in allowing himself to be cheated by empty promises; and undoubtedly the Egyptians were liberal in promising mountains of gold, though they gave nothing in reality. But as we shall find that he speaks of the Egyptians, soon afterwards, in a particular manner, I have no doubt that here he ridicules Hezekiah, as if he fed the expectation of the people by empty boasting, while he was not provided with military preparations.<div eID="gen47184" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.36.5" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen47182" osisID="Isa.36.5" type="section"/>
entries.2209078cd956ba37d030e4e92b7517e02b76cb1a: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.36.6" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.36.6" sID="gen47187" type="section"/> <div sID="gen47188" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">6.</hi><hi type="italic"> Behold, thou hast trusted in, that broken staff of reed. </hi>This is probably separate from the former verse; for, having formerly said that the eloquence by which he flatters the people is all that Hezekiah possesses, and having inferred from this that his confidence is exceedingly foolish, he now comes to other particulars. He employs every method for shaking the hearts of the people, that all, being stunned, may absolutely surrender.
